correspondences.rationale: Both denote failure of a transmitting optical laser that removes its emitted channel and causes remote signal loss.
Both denote a complete card-level hardware failure that removes traffic and monitoring and may mask subordinate alarms.
Both describe receiver-local deterioration causing errors while the shared optical path and other receivers remain normal.
Both denote a physical fibre break that interrupts light propagation to downstream equipment.
Both denote complete amplifier failure, whether in the pump or unit, producing no output and loss of all carried channels.
Both denote disconnection of an optical patch lead at a multiplex-section input, removing received light.
Both denote failure or blockage of one WSS ingress that blocks all channels on its ROADM degree while other degrees remain unaffected.
Both denote excessive or sharply increased fibre attenuation that lowers received level and degrades or loses the signal.
Both describe increased amplifier noise or noise figure that reduces downstream OSNR.
Both denote increased differential group delay on the optical path.
Both denote WSS passband misalignment that impairs one channel despite potentially normal measured power.
Both denote a rapid polarization transient exceeding coherent-receiver tracking capability.
Both denote connector contamination that introduces optical loss or reflection and degrades a channel.
Both are wildcard probable-cause categories representing any underlying failure.
Both denote partial amplifier gain loss causing weak output and reduced channel OSNR.
Both denote progressive pump deterioration requiring increased drive current to preserve gain.
Both denote wavelength-dependent non-flat gain that leaves band-edge channels weaker.
Both denote OTN cross-connect fabric failure interrupting traversing ODUs and propagating AIS.
Both denote an erroneous ODU cross-connect that routes one ODU to the wrong destination without an optical symptom.
Both denote failure of a client port or its optic, taking down the associated service.
Both denote gradual unintended WSS attenuation change that lowers routed-channel power.
Both denote absence of optical energy at the expected receiver input.
Both denote the G.798 digital loss-of-signal defect asserted by the receiver.
Both denote loss of OTU frame synchronization or alignment.
Both denote the observed state that a local equipment card or unit is nonfunctional because of hardware failure.
Both denote suppression of secondary traffic alarms by a dominant equipment alarm.
Both are broad received-signal impairment states covering low power, poor OSNR, DGD, filtering, receiver penalty, or margin loss.
Both denote appearance of pre-FEC errors once signal degradation exceeds the applicable margin or threshold.
Both denote polarization variation faster than the receiver can track.
Both denote seconds containing one or more transmission errors.
Both denote downstream insertion of ODU-AIS as an OTU-defect consequent action.
Both denote sending backward defect indication toward the remote transmitter.
Both denote far-end loss of the particular optical channel emitted by a failed transmitter.
The VB concept is a generic loss state whose stated applications include received traffic; the VA concept is that specific application.
Both denote absence of telemetry and status reporting from a failed card or unit.
Both denote errors confined to one receiver rather than shared by the path or other receivers.
Both denote unaffected optical-path or other-channel operation.
Both denote a backward report that the far end detected a defect in the locally transmitted signal.
Both denote local diagnostic detection of a transmit-laser fault.
Both denote a detected internal hardware defect affecting an equipment card.
VA automatic gain control and VB constant-gain mode both adjust pump drive to preserve configured amplifier gain.
Both denote reduced aggregate optical power arriving at an amplifier input.
Both denote reduced OSNR across every channel affected by a common amplifier or line impairment.
Both denote a unit or amplifier output from which no optical light emerges.
Both express that an OSC failure is terminated locally and does not propagate to the following section.
Both denote normal measured channel power despite a separate signal-quality impairment.
Both denote increasing pump drive current to maintain amplifier gain.
Both denote the eventual AMP_PUMP_EOL indication reached after pump ageing.
Both denote band-edge channels arriving or leaving at lower power than the others because of gain tilt.
Both denote failure to receive the OSC on the relevant fibre section.
Both denote the amplifier-failure signature of input light being present while output is dark.
Both denote measured amplifier gain more than 2 dB from its configured target or set point.
Both denote pump drive current exceeding 120% of its beginning-of-life value.
Both denote an OTN switch carrying ODU-AIS onward on every relevant cross-connected ODU.
Both denote receipt or presence of the standardized ODU alarm-indication signal.
An ODU routed to the wrong endpoint is observed there as an ODU delivered from an unexpected source.
Both denote loss of availability of the associated client service.
Both denote a service configured with redundant working and protection paths.
Both denote availability of at least one defect-free branch for the selector.
Both denote only a brief service interruption while protection selection occurs.
Both denote interruption of every ODU traversing a failed switch fabric.
Both denote forwarding AIS on affected ODU connections after a fabric or upstream defect.
Both denote delivery or cross-connection of one ODU to an unintended endpoint.
Both denote normal optical power and quality despite a logical ODU-routing defect.
Both denote the failed state of a client port or its associated optic.
Both describe a degree-wide incoming impairment persisting after the node on each independently routed channel.
Both denote an upstream power reduction within the node's available re-levelling range.
Both denote restoration of incoming channel power to its target at the node.
Both denote persistence of the OSNR penalty after optical power has been restored.
Both denote upstream attenuation exceeding the node's compensation range.
Both denote an impairment or property traversing a node without relevant alteration.
Both denote optical power below the expected target, including the WSS-drift channel case.
Both denote reduced channel recoverability or margin independently of absolute optical power.
Both denote all channels on one ROADM degree being prevented from passing.
Both denote continued normal operation on ROADM degrees other than the failed one.
Both denote monitored optical power at a receiver input.
Both denote the performance counter for seconds containing transmission errors.
Both denote monitored or estimated optical signal-to-noise ratio.
Both denote bit-error ratio measured before forward-error correction.
Both denote measured differential group delay.
Both denote the measured rate of change of the signal's state of polarization.
Both denote total aggregate optical power across all wavelengths at an amplifier input.
Both denote total aggregate optical power across all wavelengths at an amplifier output.
Both denote pump-laser drive current as a percentage of beginning-of-life current.
Both indicate whether the span supervisory channel is present or received at the input.
Both denote the client-side errored-seconds counter.
Both denote the client-side unavailable-seconds counter.
Both denote per-wavelength optical power measurements for monitored channels.
VA-TPD-400 is the vendor-specific 400G instance of VB's generic transponder resource.
VA-MXP-400 is the vendor-specific 400G instance of VB's generic muxponder resource.
VA-OTN-LC-400 is the vendor-specific 400G instance of VB's generic OTN line-card resource.
Both denote the transmit-side optical booster at the head of a multiplex section.
Both denote an inline optical amplifier installed at an intermediate site.
Both denote the receive-side amplifier at the end of a multiplex section.
Both denote an ODU-layer OTN cross-connect switch.
Both denote the generic client-facing service interface and associated optic.
Both denote a colourless, directionless, contentionless ROADM that switches wavelengths independently.

Same OTU loss-of-frame alarm.
Same OTU signal-degrade alarm.
Same OTU backward-defect indication.
Same equipment transmit-laser-failure alarm.
Same card hardware-failure alarm.
Same amplifier input-loss-of-signal alarm.
Same preamplifier OMS input-loss alarm.
Same optical supervisory-channel loss alarm.
Same amplifier failure alarm for illuminated input and dark output.
Same amplifier gain-out-of-range alarm.
Same amplifier pump end-of-life alarm.
Same client service-failure alarm.
Same indication that ODU-AIS has been received.
Same ODU backward-defect indication.
Same ODU trail-trace mismatch alarm.
Same status or alarm indicating selection of the protection path.
Same alarm indicating that the protection path is unavailable.
Same client-port equipment-failure alarm.
Same OTN cross-connect fabric-failure alarm.
Both denote the single optical wavelength directly associated with the condition.
Both denote the particular line-side channel emitted by the referenced transmitter.
Both denote traffic arriving at and processed by the referenced unit.
Both denote the unit's telemetry, status, and performance-reporting functions.
Both denote traffic-derived alarms as distinct from equipment alarms.
Both confine impact to the particular receiver rather than the shared path.
Both denote channels other than the one specifically affected.
Both denote the end-to-end optical transmission route and its common elements.
Both denote every wavelength carried through the affected common optical unit or element.
Both denote the complete affected channel set, with VA additionally making the downstream context explicit.
Both identify the single equipment instance whose local state or control action is being described.
Both denote channels near one edge of the supported optical band.
Both denote every ODU whose route traverses the referenced switch.
Both denote each member of the contextually defined affected set.
Both denote a single ODU trail rather than all ODUs.
Both denote the client-facing optical transceiver or pluggable.
Both denote the specific physical or logical client interface.
Both denote the customer-facing service carried by the port and ODU path.
Both denote every channel arriving at a ROADM on the affected degree.
Both denote channels or interfaces on ROADM degrees other than the affected one.
Both denote the remote receiver terminating the locally transmitted optical channel.
Both denote the remote endpoint opposite the current observation point.
Both denote the local observation point rather than the remote peer.
Both denote the optical receiver at which the signal's power, quality, or margin is observed.
Both denote the remote transmitting function associated with the received signal or returned BDI.
Both allow the cause to be located anywhere along the channel's upstream optical route.
Both denote the particular local equipment card associated with the alarm or metric.
Both denote a point on the route from the local endpoint toward the far end.
Both denote the direction or region following the fault in signal flow.
Both denote the upstream fibre section directly feeding the current unit.
Both denote the immediately upstream optical amplifier.
Both denote the optical connection at the input boundary of a multiplex section.
Both denote traversal of the internal OTN cross-connect path.
Both denote the ODU branch currently selected to carry the service.
Both denote either endpoint of the bidirectional service or ODU trail.
Both denote an OTN switch situated along the end-to-end ODU route.
Both denote the primary ODU path of a protected service.
Both denote the standby or protection ODU path.
Both denote the particular local port reporting or experiencing the condition.
Both locate the condition in the particular OTN switching node under examination.
Both denote the downstream side after node switching or re-levelling.
VB's contextual 'there' refers to the same local node point where VA says the blockage or action occurs.
Both indicate baseline support across applicable units without requiring an optional monitoring feature.
Both denote the optional power-monitoring entitlement required for optical power measurements.
Both denote the optional advanced-monitoring entitlement for coherent and equipment-health metrics.
Both denote the option enabling per-channel power and OSNR measurements at capable nodes.
Both classify abrupt, complete failures that immediately remove signal or service.
Both classify degradative impairments that reduce quality without constituting a complete outage.
Both classify a slowly developing warning condition that precedes likely component failure.
Same highest-priority alarm severity.
Same lower-priority alarm severity.
Same classification for informational states that do not raise a severity alarm.
Same serious alarm severity below critical.
Both specify the G.798 response to OTU frame loss: downstream ODU-AIS on every carried ODU and BDI to the far-end transmitter.
Both specify independent per-channel ROADM switching; VA additionally states the resulting persistence of ingress impairments.
